Newly settled juveniles of the red sea urchin, Mesocentrotus franciscanus, emerge from the planktonic phase with a test diameter of just 0.5 cm , a minute size that reflects the substantial energetic constraints of metamorphosis. At this stage, the wet weight at birth is approximately 2 × 10⁻⁶ grams [Wwb = approximately 2 × 10⁻⁶ grams], a value that underscores the extreme vulnerability of post-metamorphic recruits to predation and hydrodynamic disturbance. Growth during the early benthic phase is heavily influenced by the availability of crustose coralline algae, the primary settlement cue and initial food source. Laboratory rearing studies conducted at a stable water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C] have demonstrated that individuals typically achieve sexual maturity, marked by the onset of functional gametogenesis, after approximately 730 days since birth [tp = approximately 730 days since birth]. This protracted juvenile period, lasting about two years, is comparatively long among echinoids of similar adult size and likely reflects the species' strategy of investing in calcified structural defenses before allocating resources to reproductive tissues. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) recorded for reproductively active individuals averaged 21% [GSI = 21%] at a water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C].

As individuals continue to grow in the coastal kelp forests of the northeastern Pacific, their test diameter expands steadily, and the maximum size ultimately attained by large adults is approximately 19 centimeters [Li = approximately 19 centimeters]. This value represents the upper limit of test diameter observed in wild populations, with the largest specimens often found in deeper, more protected habitats where fishing pressure is reduced. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to this asymptotic size can be estimated by modeling the body as a cylindrical volume with a diameter of 19 cm and a height of 7 cm, yielding a maximum mass of roughly 2,000 grams [Wwi = roughly 2,000 grams]. This substantial body mass, among the highest recorded for any regular echinoid in the region, is supported by a diet dominated by the fronds of Macrocystis pyrifera, which the urchins graze with remarkable efficiency. Field surveys have noted that individuals approaching the maximum test diameter often exhibit thickened peristomal membranes and worn Aristotle's lanterns, signs of advanced age and prolonged feeding activity. The attainment of such a large body size is energetically costly and requires sustained access to high-quality forage over many years, a condition that is not uniformly met across the species' geographic range due to variability in kelp forest dynamics and oceanographic productivity.

The progression toward reproductive maturity in this species involves a distinct allometric shift that can be quantified through the size at which the gonads first become macroscopically visible. This developmental milestone, termed the test diameter at puberty, occurs when the individual reaches approximately 3.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 3.5 centimeters]. At this size, the urchin has already invested heavily in somatic growth but begins to divert a measurable fraction of its assimilated energy toward gamete production. The gonadosomatic index rises gradually from negligible values at sizes below 2 cm to a typical adult value of 21% [GSI = 21%] once the animal exceeds 5 to 6 cm in test diameter at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This pattern suggests that puberty is not solely a function of chronological age but is also modulated by local environmental conditions such as food availability and temperature. Comparisons with congeneric species like Mesocentrotus nudus, which matures at a slightly smaller size in Japanese waters, indicate that the pubertal threshold of 3.5 cm in M. franciscanus may reflect an adaptation to the relatively low and predictable productivity of eastern Pacific kelp forests compared to the more seasonal but nutrient-rich upwelling systems of the western Pacific.

Longevity in Mesocentrotus franciscanus has been the subject of considerable scientific interest, particularly because tagging studies and radiocarbon dating of test plates have revealed that some individuals can persist for exceptionally long periods. Under optimal conditions, the maximum recorded lifespan extends to approximately 50 years [am = approximately 50 years], a figure derived from mark-recapture data collected at a water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C] in the more productive southern portions of its range. However, some of the oldest individuals recovered from deep rocky reefs in British Columbia have been estimated to exceed 200 years, making this species one of the longest-lived of all marine invertebrates. This extraordinary longevity is accompanied by negligible senescence in reproductive output, as gravid females from age classes well beyond the typical reproductive peak continue to spawn viable gametes. The trade-off for such extended survival appears to be a relatively low annual growth rate once the asymptotic test diameter of 19 cm [Li = 19 cm] is approached, with annual increments in test size dropping to less than 0.5 cm per year in the largest size classes. The combination of exceptional lifespan and indeterminate growth potential allows M. franciscanus to buffer against years of poor recruitment by maintaining a large and fecund adult population that can exploit sporadic favorable conditions for larval settlement.

Reproductive investment in this species is tightly coupled to the seasonal availability of phytoplankton, which supplies the nutritional basis for planktotrophic larval development. Field studies conducted at a sustained temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C] have characterized the timing of sexual maturation relative to the start of independent life, showing that approximately 2 years after birth [tp = approximately 2 years after birth] is the typical interval required for an individual to reach puberty. Once adult body size is achieved, the gonadosomatic index stabilizes at 21% [GSI = 21%], though this ratio can fluctuate seasonally by as much as 50% depending on forage conditions and the timing of spawning events at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. The energetic cost of producing a single spawning batch is substantial; the wet weight at birth for each fertilized ovum is minuscule, near 2 millionths of a gram (2 × 10⁻⁶ grams) [Wwb = 2 × 10⁻⁶ grams], but the cumulative output of a large female over a single reproductive season can represent a significant fraction of her body mass. Adult individuals occupying the uppermost size classes, those approaching the ultimate wet weight of 2,000 grams [Wwi = 2,000 grams], are disproportionately important contributors to population fecundity because their gonad volume scales allometrically with body size. This size-dependent fecundity, coupled with extreme longevity, creates a reproductive portfolio in which a few very old, very large individuals may account for the majority of viable offspring entering the plankton in any given year, a demographic structure that confers considerable resilience to the population despite episodic recruitment failures.
